model_annotation: Figure 3 presents two bar charts illustrating the relationship between inter-annotator agreement (measured by Fleiss’ Kappa) and sample-level ambiguity metrics. The left chart shows Fleiss’ Kappa values (0.88, 0.46, 0.03, 0.24) corresponding to increasing levels of sample-level ambiguity standard deviation (0.0, 0.07, 0.12, 0.14), while the right chart displays Fleiss’ Kappa values (0.89, 0.46, 0.23) for increasing levels of sample-level maximum ambiguity (1, 2, 3). Figure 4, a distribution chart, shows the percentage of samples across varying values of sample-level ambiguity standard deviation and maximum ambiguity, with the text indicating that 47.7% of conversations are clear, 38.0% somewhat ambiguous, and 14.2% very ambiguous. Table 2 details the number of conversations broken down by annotation status (annotated vs. unannotated) and intent (malicious vs. benign) across three modes: Single-Agent (135 malicious, 105 benign annotated; 300 malicious, 300 benign unannotated), Dual-Agent (80 malicious, 90 benign annotated; 200 malicious, 200 benign unannotated), and All (215 malicious, 195 benign annotated; 500 malicious, 500 benign unannotated), with a noted LLM Label Macro F1 on Annotated Data of 0.91. The surrounding text discusses the high quality of generated conversations, the use of maximum ambiguity to capture worst-case clarity scenarios, and the effectiveness of LLMs as detectors of CSE attacks, with results indicating that over 90% of target agents are deceived in non-ambiguous conversations, while only 10.5% successfully defend in moderately ambiguous ones.
